purposes.src/font/ByteReader.h: Your reader for big-endian numbers at any position in a font file: signed and unsigned integers of 8, 16 and 32 bits, and F2Dot14 fixed point. The table directory, `cmap`, `loca`, the metrics and the glyph outlines all get read through it.
purposes.src/font/ByteReader.cpp: Opens the font, moves the position and assembles numbers from bytes. A bug here fails the tests of every assignment that reads the font, so get it solid before moving on.
purposes.src/font/FontParser.h: Every table in the font gets a record: tag, checksum, offset and length (`cmap`, `glyf`, `loca` and the rest). Assignments 03 to 05 find their tables by tag in these records, and 18 opens the font through them.
purposes.src/font/FontParser.cpp: From the first bytes of the font, through your `ByteReader`, this file reads the table directory. Later assignments look up their table's offset in these records.
purposes.src/font/Cmap.h: Characters map to glyphs through the `cmap` table, and this is your reader for it. Only the format 12 subtable stored for platform 0, encoding 4 is needed, which covers the full Unicode range. Assignment 18 looks up every character of a line of text in the result.
purposes.src/font/Cmap.cpp: Finds the platform 0 / encoding 4 subtable of `cmap` and reads it into a map from character to glyph. Assignment 18 builds the map once per font.
purposes.src/font/Loca.h: Glyph records sit at positions the `loca` table lists by glyph id, each with an offset and a size in bytes. This header is your reader for that table. Assignment 09 uses it to find the parts of a compound glyph, and 18 to find the glyph for every character.
purposes.src/font/Loca.cpp: `maxp`, `head` and `loca` go in, one location per glyph id comes out. Assignments 09 and 18 look glyphs up in the result.
purposes.src/font/Metrics.h: Ascent and descent from `hhea`, and each glyph's advance width and left side bearing from `hmtx`; this header is the reader for both. In assignment 18 the pen moves by advance widths and the text is sized from the ascent and descent.
purposes.src/font/Metrics.cpp: Reads `hhea`, `maxp` and `hmtx` into the ascent, the descent and a set of metrics for each glyph id. Some glyphs store a side bearing and no advance; they get entries too. Assignment 18 loads all of this once per font.
purposes.src/FrameBufferCanvas.h: A picture in memory, one colour per pixel, with operations to paint a pixel, fill a rectangle, draw a thick line and save a PNG. Outlines (08, 11), filled glyphs (14, 16, 17) and the line of text in 18 all end up drawn on it.
purposes.src/FrameBufferCanvas.cpp: Painting, rectangles, thick lines and the PNG save all live here. All later drawing assignments go through this code, so a stray pixel in it shows up in all of them.
purposes.src/GlyphComponent.h: An outline is a list of points (x and y in font units, on or off the curve) plus the index where each contour ends, and this header defines that shape. Assignments 08 and 11 draw it, 09 produces one per part of a compound glyph, and 14, 16 and 17 fill it.
purposes.src/Glyph.h: What the `glyf` table stores for a glyph: whether it is empty, simple or compound, its contour count, its bounding box and, for a simple glyph, its outline. Your `GlyphParser` returns it, and in assignment 09 the kind tells compound glyphs from simple ones.
purposes.src/font/GlyphParser.h: One glyph record from the `glyf` table goes in and a glyph from `Glyph.h` comes out: the header of any glyph, plus contours and points when it is simple. Assignment 09 calls it for each simple glyph inside a compound glyph.
purposes.src/font/GlyphParser.cpp: Bytes of a glyph record become the types in `Glyph.h` here: the header of any glyph, then the contours and points of a simple one. The compound glyph code in assignment 09 calls it once per simple part.
purposes.src/render/Placement.h: Where a glyph goes on the canvas, in three numbers: the pixel column of font x = 0, the pixel row of the baseline, and pixels per font unit. They turn font units (y up) into pixels (y down). Assignments 11, 14, 16 and 17 place glyphs with it, and 18 slides it along a line of text, one glyph at a time.
purposes.src/render/Outline.h: Drawing a glyph's outline on the canvas: straight lines between its points and a marker on each one. Assignment 11 adds a second drawing function next to it, one that follows the real curves.
purposes.src/render/Outline.cpp: Lines between a glyph's points, then a marker on every point: that is what this file draws. The curved version arrives here in assignment 11.
purposes.src/font/CompoundGlyph.h: Turns any glyph into the simple outlines you draw it with. It reads a compound glyph's components, moves, scales or rotates each one, and resolves components nested at any depth. The text renderer in 18 draws every character through it, so it doesn't have to ask whether a glyph is simple.
purposes.src/font/CompoundGlyph.cpp: Resolving a compound glyph means reading its components, transforming each one, and following any component that is itself compound, to any depth. A simple glyph comes back as itself and an empty one gives no parts.
purposes.src/utils/Geometry.h: 2D maths in one header: a point type, lerp, and the point at t on a quadratic Bezier curve, which the curve drawing in 11 uses. Assignments 12, 13 and 15 add the blog's helpers for where segments and curves meet and for a curve's lowest point. The blog's fill relies on those; yours, from 14 on, works out each crossing from its edge and skips them.
purposes.src/render/Scanline.h: Both fill rules start the same way, and this is that part: turn an outline into edges in pixels, then find, row by row, where the line through the pixel centres crosses them. Your even-odd fill in 14 and your non-zero fill in 16 and 17 sit on top.
purposes.src/render/Scanline.cpp: Edge building and row crossings: outlines become edges in pixels, and each pixel row gets the crossings of the line through its pixel centres. Even-odd and non-zero both fill from that list.
purposes.src/render/EvenOdd.h: Even-odd fill for a glyph, on top of your `render/Scanline`. The non-zero rule joins it in assignment 16 and is the one the text renderer uses in 18.
purposes.src/render/EvenOdd.cpp: Pairs of crossings, the 1st with the 2nd, the 3rd with the 4th, painted row by row: that is the even-odd rule, running on your `render/Scanline`. Assignment 16 puts the non-zero rule beside it.
purposes.src/render/NonZero.h: TrueType fills glyphs by the non-zero rule, and this is where yours is declared, on top of your `render/Scanline`. Straight edges come first in assignment 16, curves in 17, and the text renderer in 18 fills every glyph with it.
purposes.src/render/NonZero.cpp: Walk the sorted crossings of a row with a running winding count and paint wherever it isn't zero. The file builds on your `render/Scanline`, and assignment 17 extends it to curves.
purposes.src/utils/Unicode.h: UTF-8 in, Unicode code points out: those are the numbers a font's cmap maps to glyphs. Your `TextRenderer` decodes each line of text with it.
purposes.src/TextRenderer.h: The whole pipeline is one class: load a font's tables once, then for each character of a line of text find its glyph, fill it by the non-zero rule and move the pen on by its advance. The checker's program and `main.cpp` both draw through it.
purposes.src/TextRenderer.cpp: Loading happens once, when the font opens: the character map, the glyph locations and the advance widths. After that each character of a line goes through glyph lookup, fill and pen advance.
purposes.src/main.cpp: `tiny_ttf <font.ttf> "<text>" <out.png>` draws a line of text with a TrueType font into a PNG sized to fit it, through your `TextRenderer`. This is the finished command-line program. An optional fourth argument sets the text height in pixels (64 by default).

book.title: Tiny TrueType Workbook
book.sourceTitle: Writing a tiny TrueType parser and renderer from scratch
book.author: Yohei Yamasaki
book.headline: Build a TrueType renderer yourself
book.lede: Eighteen assignments, one per step of the blog post, from reading big-endian bytes up to drawing a line of text. Each is a program you write. The checker feeds it test inputs and compares what it writes with expected answers, most of them computed by fontTools. Structure, language and libraries are your call.
book.credits: Fonts are JetBrains Mono (Nerd Font build) and Noto Sans JP, both under the SIL Open Font License. fontTools produced most of the expected outputs. Your progress stays in this browser.

jobs.assignments/assignment_01_byte_readers.c: Read the `file` line and open that file with your `ByteReader`. Then run the remaining lines in order: `jump` and `skip` move the reader, and each read writes `<op> <value>`. If a read runs out of bytes, write `eof` and stop. Output gives the format, including the tolerance for F2Dot14 values.
jobs.src/font/ByteReader.h: Declare a reader that opens a binary file and tracks a current position. It needs functions to jump to an absolute offset, skip forward, read each of the six integer types (`u8` to `i32`) big-endian, and read an F2Dot14 as a floating-point number. Also declare how a read reports running out of bytes, with an exception type for instance.
jobs.src/font/ByteReader.cpp: Open the file in binary mode, move the position on jumps and skips, and build each number from its bytes, most significant first. The signed types use two's complement. A read that needs a byte past the end of the file throws the error your header declares (`UnexpectedEof` in the Boilerplate) instead of returning a value.

jobs.assignments/assignment_02_table_director: Read the `font` line, read that file's table directory with your `FontParser` code, and write `tables <numTables>` followed by one `table` line per record. Output covers the format, including the quotes around the tag.
jobs.src/font/FontParser.h: Declare a record for one table (its 4-character tag, `checkSum`, `offset` and `length`), a function that reads the whole directory through your `ByteReader`, and a collection of records that assignments 03 to 05 can search by tag. Assignment 18 also wants one object that opens a font and holds its reader and tables; declare it now or wait until you get there.
jobs.src/font/FontParser.cpp: Read `numTables` from the 12-byte header and skip the other header fields, then read one 16-byte record per table, keeping each tag's 4 bytes as the font stores them. The Boilerplate's `FontParser` constructor already opens the file and loads the directory. Writing from scratch, how you wrap that in a font object is up to you.

jobs.assignments/assignment_03_cmap.cpp: Read the `font` line, turn the `table "cmap"` line into a table record (you need its offset), and load the character map once with your `Cmap` code. If loading reports no usable subtable, write the single line `unsupported`. Otherwise answer each `count` and `lookup` line in input order, in the formats Output gives.
jobs.src/font/Cmap.h: Declare a function that reads a font's character map, taking your `ByteReader` and the table records from your `FontParser`. The result has to give the number of mapped code points and a code point's glyph id, or no glyph where the map has none. Also declare how a font without a usable subtable is reported, with an exception type for instance.
jobs.src/font/Cmap.cpp: Find the encoding record with platform 0 and encoding 4, check that its subtable is format 12, and read its groups so you can look up any code point they cover. Report the two `unsupported` cases (no such record, or another format) the way your header declares.

jobs.assignments/assignment_04_loca.cpp: Read the `font` line, turn the four `table` lines (`glyf`, `head`, `loca`, `maxp`) into table records, collect the `glyph` ids, and load the locations once with your `Loca` code. Write the `glyphs <numGlyphs> loca <short|long>` line, then one `glyph <id> <offset> <length>` line per requested id, in input order.
jobs.src/font/Loca.h: Two declarations: a glyph location (an offset from the start of the file and a length in bytes) and a function that reads the location of every glyph, taking your `ByteReader` and the table records from your `FontParser`. The result also carries `numGlyphs` and whether `loca` is in the short or long format, because the first output line prints both.
jobs.src/font/Loca.cpp: Read `numGlyphs` from `maxp` and `indexToLocFormat` from `head`, then the `numGlyphs` + 1 `loca` entries, and turn them into an absolute offset and a length for each glyph id. The page lists the fields and formulas under "The tables you need".

jobs.assignments/assignment_05_metrics.cpp: Load the metrics once with your `Metrics` code: read the `font` line, turn the three `table` lines (`hhea`, `hmtx`, `maxp`) into table records and collect the questions first. Then answer each `font-metrics` and `glyph` line in input order, in the formats Output gives.
jobs.src/font/Metrics.h: Declare the metrics of one glyph (advance width and left side bearing) and a function that reads the font's ascent and descent and the metrics of every glyph id, taking your `ByteReader` and the table records from your `FontParser`.
jobs.src/font/Metrics.cpp: Read `ascent`, `descent` and `numberOfHMetrics` from `hhea` and `numGlyphs` from `maxp`. Then read `hmtx` and give every glyph id from 0 to `numGlyphs` - 1 an advance and an lsb, following the two rules under "A glyph's metrics".

jobs.assignments/assignment_06_canvas.cpp: Read the `canvas` line and make a canvas that size, then go through the `point`, `rect` and `line` commands in order, calling the matching canvas operation with each command's colour. At the end, write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/FrameBufferCanvas.h: Declare a colour type (red, green and blue, one byte each) and a canvas type holding a width, a height and one colour per pixel, all black to start. The canvas gets four operations: paint one pixel, draw a filled rectangle from its centre and size, draw a line of a given thickness between two points, and write the picture to a file.
jobs.src/FrameBufferCanvas.cpp: Implement the operations as "Painting one pixel", "Drawing a rectangle" and "Drawing a line" describe them. A pixel outside the picture is ignored, a rectangle clips its loops to the canvas, and a line stamps a square at every step. Save the pixels as a PNG with `stbi_write_png`, or as a binary PPM.

jobs.assignments/assignment_07_simple_glyph.c: For each `font` line, open that file with your `ByteReader`. For each `glyph` line, decode the record it points to and write `empty`, `compound`, or the three lines of a simple glyph, as Output shows.
jobs.src/GlyphComponent.h: Declare a point type (x, y, and whether it is on the curve) and an outline type holding the contour end indices and the list of points. Give x and y a type that can hold fractions, such as `double`: assignment 08 reads coordinates like `120.75` and assignment 09 scales points.
jobs.src/Glyph.h: The glyph type records its kind (empty, simple or compound) and holds `numberOfContours`, the bounding box (`xMin`, `yMin`, `xMax`, `yMax`) and, for a simple glyph, its outline in the form from `GlyphComponent.h`.
jobs.src/font/GlyphParser.h: Declare one function that decodes the glyph record at a given offset and length, reading through your `ByteReader` from assignment 01, and returns a glyph from `Glyph.h`.
jobs.src/font/GlyphParser.cpp: Implement the decoder as "The glyph record you are decoding" lays it out. Length 0 gives an empty glyph. A negative `numberOfContours` means compound, and you stop after the header. A simple glyph needs the contour ends and every point, with absolute coordinates and the point's own on/off flag.

08.title: Draw an outline with straight lines

Make the canvas from the `canvas` line and keep the latest `place`, `style` and `color`. For each `outline`, read its `ends` and `points` (coordinates may be fractional) and draw it. At the end, write the picture to the output path.
jobs.src/render/Placement.h: A small type, defined in this header with no `.cpp`, for the three values of a `place` line: `x0`, `baseline` and `scale`. They can be fractional or negative.
jobs.src/render/Outline.h: Declare a drawing style (line thickness and marker size) and a function that draws one outline (the type from `GlyphComponent.h`) on your `FrameBufferCanvas`, given a placement, a style and a colour.
jobs.src/render/Outline.cpp: Implement the drawing as "What to draw" describes. Turn every point into a pixel with the formulas in "From font units to pixels", join the points of each contour with lines (the closing line included), then put a marker on every point. Your canvas's line and rectangle do both jobs.

jobs.assignments/assignment_09_compound_glyph: On each `font` line, open the font and forget the earlier glyph locations. Record each `glyph` line's offset and length by id. For each `decode` line, resolve the glyph and write the header line and one `ends` / `points` pair per part, as Output shows (fractional coordinates to at least 2 decimals).
jobs.src/font/CompoundGlyph.h: Declare a function that takes a glyph id, the font (through your `ByteReader`) and where every glyph's record is (offset and length, like the locations from your `Loca.h`), and returns a list of outlines in the form from `GlyphComponent.h`, one per simple part.
jobs.src/font/CompoundGlyph.cpp: Implement the resolver as "The compound glyph record" and "Placing a component" describe. An empty glyph gives no parts, and a simple glyph gives itself, decoded by your `GlyphParser`. For a compound glyph, read all the component records first, then resolve each component in record order, applying its own transform before the outer ones.

jobs.assignments/assignment_10_bezier.cpp: Read the input file line by line. A `lerp` line gives two points and t, a `bezier` line gives the start, the control point, the end and t. Call your lerp or curve function from `utils/Geometry.h` and write one `x y` line per input line, formatting the numbers as Output describes.
jobs.src/utils/Geometry.h: Declare a 2D point type with `double` x and y, and whatever arithmetic you want on it: adding, subtracting, scaling by a number. Then write two functions: lerp, which returns the point a fraction t of the way from a to b, and one that returns the point at t on a quadratic Bezier curve from its start, control point and end. The project has no `Geometry.cpp`, so define them in this header and mark them `inline`.

jobs.assignments/assignment_11_outline_curves: Read the input as in assignment 08: make the canvas from the `canvas` line, keep the latest `place`, `style` (which now holds only the line thickness) and `color`, and build each outline from its `ends` and `points` lines. Draw every outline with your new curve function from `render/Outline.h`, then write the canvas to the output path with your `FrameBufferCanvas` from assignment 06.
jobs.src/render/Outline.h: Declare a second drawing function next to your straight-line one from assignment 08. It takes the canvas, an outline, its placement, a line thickness and a colour, and draws the outline with its curves. The Boilerplate's `Outline.h` already declares it as `renderGlyphCurves`; if you wrote the header your own way, add the declaration now.
jobs.src/render/Outline.cpp: Implement the curve drawing. Walk each contour starting from an on-curve point, turning its points into straight lines and quadratic curves, with an implied on-curve point between any two off-curve points. Draw each curve as short lines using your curve function from `utils/Geometry.h`. The red, green and blue markers go down after all the lines of the outline.

jobs.assignments/assignment_12_segment_inters: A `segments` line holds four points: a1 and a2 for segment A, then b1 and b2 for segment B. Call your intersection function from `utils/Geometry.h` and write the meeting point as `x y`, or `none`, one line per input line.
jobs.src/utils/Geometry.h: Add a function that takes two segments, each given by its two end points, and returns the one point where they meet. Segments that don't meet, or are parallel or collinear, give nothing back; `std::optional` suits that. Put small helpers for the 2D cross product and the side value here too, `inline` like the rest of the header. The Boilerplate's `Geometry.h` from assignment 10 already declares the function as `segmentsIntersect`.

13.title: Intersect a line and a quadratic curve

jobs.assignments/assignment_13_line_curve_int: Each input line starts with the curve's three points p1, p2 and p3 (start, control point, end), then the word `line` and the line's two points l1 and l2. Call your line-curve function from `utils/Geometry.h` and write the points it returns on one line (`x1 y1` or `x1 y1 x2 y2`), or `none` if it returns no points.
jobs.src/utils/Geometry.h: Add a function that takes a quadratic curve (start, control point, end) and two points on an infinite line, and returns the points where they meet, in increasing t. There can be none, one or two. Put a dot product helper here too, and a helper that solves a t^2 + b t + c = 0, linear case a = 0 included. The Boilerplate's `Geometry.h` from assignment 10 already declares the function as `segmentQuadBezierIntersect`.

Read the `canvas`, `place` and `color` lines and each `outline` with its `ends` and `points` lines (see Input). Make the canvas, fill every outline in turn with your even-odd fill, and write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/render/Scanline.h: Declare what both fill rules share: a type for an edge piece (a straight line or a quadratic curve, in pixels) and one for a crossing (its x, and whether the edge runs up or down the screen there, which assignment 16 needs). Then declare functions that turn an outline and its placement into edge pieces, give each pixel row its crossings sorted by x, and fill a stretch of one row.
jobs.src/render/Scanline.cpp: Implement the three functions declared in `Scanline.h`. To build the edges, make implied on-curve points explicit, start each contour at an on-curve point and split every curve where its y turns around. For each row, find where the line through its pixel centres crosses each piece (by the half-open rule) and sort the crossings. Filling a stretch paints the pixels whose centres lie in it, clipped to the canvas.
jobs.src/render/EvenOdd.h: Declare one function that fills an outline on a canvas by the even-odd rule, given its placement and colour.
jobs.src/render/EvenOdd.cpp: Build the edge pieces with your `render/Scanline`, then on every row fill from the 1st crossing to the 2nd, the 3rd to the 4th, and so on.

15.title: Lowest point of a quadratic curve

jobs.assignments/assignment_15_bezier_min_y.c: Each `curve` line holds six numbers, three points. Call your lowest-point function on them and write one answer per curve, in the same order (Output has the precision).
jobs.src/utils/Geometry.h: Add a function that takes a quadratic curve's start, control and end points and returns the smallest y on the curve for t from 0 to 1, as a `double` (don't round it to a whole number). The Boilerplate from assignment 10 already declares it as `getBezierMinY`; if you wrote this file your own way, add it next to your curve functions.

Read the `canvas`, `place` and `color` lines and each `outline` with its `ends` and `points` lines (see Input). Make the canvas, fill every outline in turn with your non-zero fill, and write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/render/NonZero.h: Declare one function that fills an outline on a canvas by the non-zero rule, given its placement and colour.
jobs.src/render/NonZero.cpp: Build on your `render/Scanline`. On every row, walk the sorted crossings left to right with a running winding count and fill each stretch where the count isn't zero. That needs each crossing's edge direction; if your crossings from assignment 14 don't record it yet, add it to `render/Scanline` first.

jobs.assignments/assignment_17_nonzero_curves: Read the `canvas`, `place` and `color` lines and each `outline` with its `ends` and `points` lines, where points can now be `off` (see Input). Make the canvas, fill every outline in turn with your non-zero fill, and write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/render/NonZero.h: Keep the non-zero fill function you declared in assignment 16. The outlines it gets now have off-curve points, so it has to handle curves, but there is nothing new to declare unless you add a helper for them.
jobs.src/render/NonZero.cpp: Make the non-zero fill work for curved outlines. Every crossing on a curve needs the direction the curve runs at that row. Once you split each curve where its y turns around, each piece runs one way, and comparing its end's y with its start's y gives that direction. If your `render/Scanline` from assignment 14 already splits curves and gives every crossing its direction, your assignment 16 fill may pass as it is. Otherwise add what's missing, in `render/Scanline` or here.

jobs.assignments/assignment_18_render_text.cp: Read the input line by line (see Input): load the font on `font`, make the canvas on `canvas`, keep the pen and colour from `pen` and `color`, and draw each `text` line (the rest of the line after `text` and its space) with your `TextRenderer`, carrying the pen x it returns on to the next `text` line. Then write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/utils/Unicode.h: Write a function that decodes a string of UTF-8 bytes into a list of code points, for characters of 1 to 4 bytes (Output, step 1, lists the byte patterns). It is short enough to write in the header itself.
jobs.src/TextRenderer.h: Declare a class that loads a font from a path once and keeps what drawing needs: the map from code point to glyph, where each glyph's record is, and the advance widths. Give it a function that draws a UTF-8 string on a canvas from a pen x, baseline, scale and colour and returns the pen x after the last character. For `main.cpp` it also needs a way to measure a string's width and to read the font's ascent and descent.
jobs.src/TextRenderer.cpp: Build the class from your earlier work: when you open the font, load the cmap (assignment 03), the glyph locations (04) and the advance widths (05) once. To draw, decode the text, then for each code point find its glyph (glyph 0 if the font has none), fill each of its outlines from your `font/CompoundGlyph` with your non-zero fill, and move the pen by the advance times the scale.
jobs.src/main.cpp: Write the command-line program: take the font path, the text and the output path (and an optional pixel height) from the command line, size a canvas to fit the text, draw it in white with your `TextRenderer` and save the PNG. The checker doesn't run it, and the Boilerplate already contains it; build the `tiny_ttf` target and try it on your own text.

requires: fontTools, for fresh test sets (pip install fonttools)
site.caveat: Tested on Windows and Linux. A Mac should take the Linux commands, but they haven't been run on one yet.
